title: Echoes Rising
author: Sandra Boyle

chapters.title: Chapter 1 - Fragments
chapters.content:
Chapter 1 - Fragments

Most memory reconstruction sessions start the same way: a tremor in the client’s voice, a hesitant glance at the console, then the long exhale as they finally allow the machine to access the places they’ve been told to forget. My job is to guide them through the fragments—nothing more. I’m not a therapist. I’m not a detective. I’m certainly not a savior.

I’m an echoist. I restore echoes; what’s already there.

This morning’s client, a woman in her sixties, came in to recover a piece of her husband’s last week of life. It had been wiped to alleviate grief, per government regulation after partner loss. She wasn’t supposed to want it back. But they always do.

I held her hand steady while the sync cables adjusted to her cortex band. “You may feel a light pulse,” I said, keeping my tone neutral. “Like static against your scalp.”

Her eyes fluttered shut. “Will I see him?”

“You’ll feel him first. If the file is intact.”

It was. For seventeen seconds, she saw a worn flannel shirt and a rain-warped window. He had been singing—off-key, badly. She wept in silence. When it ended, she nodded once and stood without needing help.

Those were the easy ones. Sad, yes. But clean. Human. Predictable.

The next client wasn’t on my roster.

I was filing the woman’s exit statement when I saw the man in the waiting area, seated stiffly near the corner recharge panel. He wasn’t pacing like the anxious ones did. He was still. Too still.

His eyes found mine like he’d been awaiting the exact second I’d look up.

“Can I help you?” I asked, approaching cautiously. He wasn’t a regular. And he hadn’t scanned in. My console hadn’t pinged.

“Are you the one they call Kess?” he asked, voice low and dry.

“Lira Kess, yes. Do you have an appointment?”

He shook his head. “They told me to ask for you specifically.”

I didn’t like that. My name wasn’t listed anywhere public.

“Who told you?”

He hesitated. “A technician in New Terra. She said you handle the... unusual cases.”

I frowned. “This isn’t a walk-in clinic. You need clearance, intake approval—”

“It’s about my daughter.”

That stopped me.

“I lost her. Not in the way people mean. I lost her in my head. There’s... nothing. Not a sound. Not a smell. But I remember loving her.”

I took a step back and tapped the console panel on the wall. “Name?”

“Jonah Vale.”

I initiated a soft search. Nothing came up in the Memory Recovery Requests. No loss certification. No familial data. No one filed as next-of-kin. His profile listed no dependents, no guardianship, no parental flags.

“You’re not listed as having a child,” I said carefully.

“I know.”

I blinked. “Then how—”

He reached into the inner pocket of his coat and pulled out a small photograph. A real one. Paper. Matte finish. The edges were curled, the corners soft from wear. It showed a girl, maybe six or seven, with wind-blown hair and two missing front teeth. She was laughing. Someone had written a name on the back in faded ink: Lina.

Jonah’s fingers brushed the photo’s edge, almost reverently. “They took everything else,” he said quietly. “But this… I found it years later, tucked behind an old access panel in my mother’s studio. She must’ve hidden it—kept one piece safe, even when I couldn’t. “He looked up. “The filters missed it. Guess they weren’t trained to search for paper ghosts.”

The image wouldn’t scan. The code strip had long worn away.

“I’ve carried this for years,” he said. “But I don’t remember taking it. Or what she liked. Or even if she’s still alive. I don’t remember her birthday. Just the ache of her absence.”

I sat down slowly.

“There’s no record of her, Mr. Vale. Not in the memory registry. Not in family data.”

“That’s why I came here.” His voice cracked now, just slightly. “I want to know why she’s missing. And if she was ever really mine.”

I hesitated. This wasn’t procedure. I was bound by strict reconstruction protocols. All memory sessions required clearance. We weren’t allowed to dive into unverified fragments, especially not from people with potential mental health flags. Memory delusion was real. So was imprint contamination.

“Sir, I’m not a recovery unit. I restore legal, recorded memories after trauma, illness, or grief protocols. I don’t investigate—”

“I’m not asking you to believe me. I’m asking you to scan me.” He slid the photo toward me. “Off the books. Just one thread. If there’s nothing there, I’ll leave.”

I stared at the photo, then at him.

Jonah Vale wasn’t twitchy or erratic. He wasn’t desperate in the usual sense. There was something calmer in his face—resignation, maybe. He already expected I’d say no.

But I didn’t.

Not yet.

I stood up and tapped the wall panel. “There’s a private sync room upstairs. No recording feed. Manual override only.”

He blinked. “You’ll do it?”

“I’ll look. That’s all. If there’s nothing to find, I can’t invent memories for you.”

“I know,” he said. “But if you find even a sliver... I need to know I didn’t imagine her.”

Upstairs, I activated the room’s analog interface—one of the last unconnected terminals we still had. The sync bands weren’t as smooth as the digital ones, but they wouldn’t alert the central archive.

He sat in the chair with the posture of someone who’d done this before.

“Any medications?” I asked.

“No.”

“Neurological implants?”

“Just a cortex stabilizer. Low dose. Prescribed two years ago.”

“For?”

“Stress and long-term data loss. It didn’t help.”

I adjusted the dials. “You may see shifts. Partial threads. Soundless loops. Don’t try to control them.”

He nodded.

I pressed start.

At first, the screen remained dark. Jonah’s brainwaves pulsed in slow, uneven rhythms—common in trauma-based memory decay. But then something shifted. A flash. A child’s laugh. A sidewalk.

I isolated the fragment.

The girl was spinning in circles, arms wide, sunlight streaking across her shoulders. She turned—briefly—and the image broke apart.

Her face.

I knew that face.

Not from my client file. Not from any case.

From somewhere behind my own eyes.

The girl looked like me.

Not exactly. Younger. A different haircut. But the same dimple. The same tilt in the smile. Like a mirror, or a cousin I’d never met.

I yanked the feed back to normal.

Jonah blinked, dazed. “Did you see her?”

“I saw... something.” I stood, heart racing. “You said you don’t remember her name?”

“Just Lina.”

I looked again at the photo on the desk.

Lina.

That was the name I used for a stuffed fox when I was six. No one knew that. It wasn’t in any file. I hadn’t said it aloud in over a decade.

“Mr. Vale, this isn’t something I can file officially. You understand that.”

He nodded. “I’m not asking for reports.”

I hesitated again, then reached for the data stick.

“I’ll run a deeper reconstruction. One pass. You’ll be present. After that, we’re done.”

His hands shook as he folded the photo back into his coat.

“Thank you,” he whispered.

I didn’t say you’re welcome. Because I wasn’t.

Because I was already afraid of what I’d find next.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - Echo Threads
chapters.content:
Chapter 2 - Echo Threads

The analog sync room on the second floor was barely used these days. It had no biometric locks, no cloud relay, no audit trail—just a heavy door, thick insulation, and an aging console that hummed like it remembered being important. The Ministry kept it for liability reasons, mostly. Occasionally, a client with a non-compatible implant would require a manual session.

Or someone like Jonah Vale.

I keyed in my override code and held the door open as he stepped inside. He looked around slowly, eyes tracing the wall panels like he was trying to memorize every shadow.

“This feels old,” he said.

“It is,” I replied. “But sometimes, old tech knows how to listen better than new.”

He sat without prompting in the chair that faced the dome-shaped receiver. I connected the sensor bands to his cortex base and attached a single skin node to the side of his temple.

“No full sync,” I said. “Just surface resonance. It’ll show neural flares if anything’s imprinted—sensory cues, emotional trails, flash tones.”

“And if there’s nothing?”

“Then you’ll feel lightheaded and disappointed.”

His mouth twitched into the faintest smile. “I’ve had worse.”

I turned away from him, suddenly conscious of the quiet hum of the room—the soft buzz of the ancient interface, the faint clicking of internal memory drivers warming up. Most echoists hated this space. It felt too analog, too exposed. But I’d always liked it. There was no automation, no intelligent feedback loop. Just input and output. Just memory and machine.

I tapped the console, and the interface blinked to life—orange and blue arcs sweeping across the screen. The software was crude by modern standards, but it still worked. I started a passive scan, fingers resting just above the emergency cut-off.

For several seconds, the display remained neutral. No emotional spikes. No memory tags. No residual patterns. I was about to end the session when something flared in the lower quadrant.

A burst of light. A spinning waveform. A pulse.

I increased sensitivity and adjusted the field parameters. Then—

The image appeared.

A child spinning in circles under open sky, her arms outstretched. Wind tugged at her hair. She was laughing, her voice trailing like music. The edges of the scene blurred and bled light, unstable but vivid. Her clothes were slightly dated—simple blue jacket, torn hem. And she wore a bracelet that caught the light with every turn.

I leaned forward involuntarily.

The face.

I knew that face.

Same cheekbones. Same dimple. Same crooked smile I tried to hide in mirrors.

It was me.

Not exactly—not certainly—but enough to raise a chill along my spine. Enough to stir something deep and half-buried in the folds of my own memory.

Jonah inhaled sharply.

“Lina,” he whispered. “That’s her.”

I turned to him. “Are you sure?”

He nodded slowly. “That laugh. I used to tell her not to spin like that. She’d get dizzy, but she said it made the world feel soft.”

The scan pulsed again, fragmenting into white static as the signal faltered. The image stuttered, then vanished.

I powered down the console.

“Was that real?” he asked quietly.

“Real enough to be dangerous,” I said, more to myself than him. “I’ve never seen neural residue that clear without a support file.”

Jonah stood, the cords disconnecting with soft clicks. “So what now?”

I stared at the blank monitor. The girl’s laughter still rang faintly in my ears. I shouldn’t have felt anything. I’d seen echoes before—faint impressions, grief-traced hallucinations, AI-stitched reconstructions. But this was different.

This one reached for me.

“There’s a deeper protocol,” I said slowly. “A mosaic reconstruction. It’s meant for layered trauma cases—clients with compound memory damage or suppressed clusters.”

Jonah’s eyes sharpened. “You think she’s still in there?”

“I think something is.”

He took a step closer. “Will you run it?”

I didn’t answer right away. My fingers hovered over the log panel. My instincts warred with my training. I was not supposed to run unverified scans, not without at least three points of legal reference, not without an observer. But I’d seen something—someone—and it had looked back.

Normally, I’d file the session into the memory cloud, tag it for review, submit it for a session ID and forensic backup. But if I did that, someone would flag it immediately. Questions would follow. Jonah would be pulled in. I’d be suspended.

I tapped a few keys and encrypted the footage.

“No logs,” I said. “No cloud backup. This stays with me.”

He nodded, and for the first time since he walked into the clinic, some of the tension in his shoulders eased.

“I’ll need to prepare the deeper scan,” I said. “Manual prep takes longer. We’ll run it tomorrow—same time.”

“And if I come back and you’ve changed your mind?”

“Then you’ll know it’s because I found something I wasn’t supposed to.”

He offered a small, haunted smile. “That’s good enough for me.”

As he turned to leave, I stayed behind in the analog room, the screen still faintly glowing from the scan’s residual energy. I stood in the quiet for several minutes, replaying the flash in my mind. The spinning girl. The laugh. The bracelet. My own face.

Then I did something I rarely do—I sat in the chair across from the console and let myself feel it. Not assess it, not catalog it. Just feel it. The ache of recognition. The terror of memory reaching for me instead of the other way around.

I ran a final sweep, locking the session behind a passcode only I knew. I renamed the file with a neutral string of code, burying it three levels deep.

Then I whispered, under my breath:

“Lina.”

And for just a moment, I swore I heard someone whisper it back.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 – False Faces
chapters.content:
Chapter 3 – False Faces

I didn’t sleep.

I told myself I was just cataloging the scan, mentally parsing the sequence frame by frame. But the truth lodged deeper. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw her—spinning, laughing, vanishing. Not Jonah’s daughter. Mine. Or at least… some reflection of me.

By dawn, I’d replayed the visual thread a hundred times in my mind. Her eyes. Her laugh. The tilt of her head as she turned. I kept asking myself if this was a coincidence, a projection of my own subconscious. But the ache in my chest told me it wasn’t.

I poured a cup of synth-coffee and sat by the low terminal in my apartment, fingers hovering over the biometric key. My access codes allowed limited backdoor entry into Ministry records—not illegal, but frowned upon when used for personal reasons. Still, I needed to see it for myself.

I navigated to my file.

Name: Lira Kess Clearance: Level 3 – Cognitive Recovery Specialist Medical Notes: Updated last month

Then I saw it—

A 12-month memory gap, listed simply as “procedural adjustment for emotional stabilization.”

Age: 6 to 7.

The note was flagged as non-editable. No therapist signature. No attending physician. Just a date, a deletion, and a Ministry watermark.

I leaned back, the coffee cooling rapidly in my hand. The blankness on the screen felt louder than any revelation. Why hadn’t I noticed this before? Why had no one ever mentioned it? And why was I only feeling the absence now, like a phantom limb starting to ache?

I remembered a recurring dream I used to have as a teenager: a girl in a red sweater standing on a playground bridge, waiting. She never spoke. I never reached her. Was it just a dream? Or a residue of something real?

I opened the secure drawer under the terminal and pulled out the old childhood keepsake box my mother insisted I take when I moved out. Most of it was junk—paper drawings, a chipped music pendant, a faded camp patch. But tucked in the bottom was a small wooden frame. Empty.

I ran my thumb across its edge. There was adhesive residue on the back, like a photo had once been mounted and removed. The faint outline of a child’s shape lingered in the dust-streaked glass. Oval face. Tilted head. Laughing mouth.

My pulse quickened.

“Lina…” I whispered.

The word hung in the air like static.

I reached for my comm.

My mother answered on the third ring. Her hair was damp, and she wore her gardening gloves like she’d just stepped in from tending the balcony herbs.

“Lira! It’s early. Is everything okay?”

“I found something strange in my medical file,” I said. “A year’s worth of memory—gone. When I was six.”

Her smile faltered. “Oh, honey, I’m sure that’s just part of the adjustment process from the trauma protocol they gave you.”

“What trauma?”

“Well, you had nightmares for a while, don’t you remember? You used to wake up screaming—something about a girl and a swing set.”

“A girl named Lina?”

My mother’s lips pressed into a tight line. She removed one glove slowly. “Lira, that was a long time ago. Your doctors did what was best. You’ve built a good life. Why dig it all up?”

“I need to know.”

She looked away from the screen. “I always thought you were better off not knowing.”

Her voice softened, almost pleading. “Some memories do more harm than good.”

The call disconnected.

No goodbye.

Just silence.

I stared at the darkened comm screen for several minutes before pushing the keepsake box aside. Then I pulled out my encrypted journal drive.

I opened a new entry.

SUBJECT: Lina – Possible Memory Residue Date: Unknown / Fragment origin unclear. Physical similarities noted. Bracelet detail matches known childhood item. Mother's deflection raises suspicion. Photo frame missing contents. Timeline gap confirmed in records. Jonah's recognition complicates theory.

I hesitated before writing the last line.

Running mosaic session anyway.

I closed the entry and sat still for a long time. Outside, the sky was a dull steel gray, and the city’s drones buzzed faintly in the distance. It felt like the world was pressing in, expectant and unreadable.

Later that day, I returned to the clinic and booked the sync chamber for a full-hour session under an anonymized ID tag. I logged it as “Layered Loss Assessment – Stage 2.” No one would question it—these slots were used for grief mapping all the time. I modified the metadata, masked the subject ID, and copied the new scan template to my personal slate.

When Jonah arrived, I met him at the back entrance.

“Are we doing this?” he asked.

I nodded. “We are.”

He followed me into the prep room, his hands visibly trembling. “I keep seeing her,” he said. “In my dreams. In crowds. It’s like the memory is hunting me.”

I paused. “You’re not the only one.”

He looked at me, searching. “What do you mean?”

I just shook my head. “Let’s get started.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4 – Fractures in the Feed
chapters.content:
Chapter 4 – Fractures in the Feed

“Again?” I muttered as the sync chamber buzzed to life, the cold press of the headset already ghosting my temples.

The low hum under my skin deepened, and the faint flicker of red light painted shadows across the floor. The air carried a faint tang of ozone and disinfectant, mingling with the mechanical thrum of the cooling fans embedded in the floor. The padded floor muffled every step, and a persistent ticking noise—like a metronome buried inside the walls—kept time with the flash of blue light.

It smelled like stale electricity and old memories, if such a scent existed., like a heartbeat just beneath the surface. I guided Jonah to the reclined chair and adjusted the neural halo around his temples. The room was analog, air-gapped, and untraceable. No data uplinks. No digital records. Just memory and nerve.

“Ready?” I asked.

Jonah gave a slow nod, eyes glassy but determined. “If she’s in there… even a piece of her…”

I didn’t need him to finish. I understood.

I activated the mosaic program manually, bypassing Ministry protocols. The machine hummed to life, its monitors displaying an array of flashing memory threads—some clear, others shadowed and incomplete.

“This will overlap resonance fields,” I explained, mostly to fill the silence. “We’ll see images from your long-term imprint and subconscious overlays. They may not always be accurate, but they will reflect emotional truth.”

Jonah closed his eyes.

The first memory opened gently: the image of a small bedroom, bathed in late-afternoon light. A child’s giggle echoed softly. A lullaby hummed by a male voice—Jonah’s. A stuffed animal clutched in tiny arms. Then bedtime stories. The low murmur of affection. A girl’s hair catching the light.

Jonah inhaled sharply, his entire body going still. “That’s her. That’s… Lina.” His voice cracked at the edges, barely more than a breath. His eyes locked on the screen, wide and unblinking, as if afraid the image might vanish if he looked away. A tremor ran through his hands, which clenched tightly on the chair’s arms until his knuckles paled. His chest rose in sharp, uneven bursts, and a wet sheen pooled along his lower lashes. For a moment, it looked like he might say more, but he just pressed a palm against the screen’s reflection, as if reaching for her. "She always spun like that... when she was happy,"

His voice cracked on the last word. A silence followed—heavy and taut, as if the memory itself was holding its breath. Jonah’s hands trembled at his sides, clenched so tight his knuckles bleached. His eyes never left the ghostly image of Lina spinning through the mosaic feed. “She used to sing, too,” he murmured, as if speaking might anchor her longer. “A broken little tune she made up. I can't remember the words. Just the feeling.”

He turned away suddenly, a stifled sound catching in his throat—part laugh, part sob. Lira watched him silently, her own breath caught between past and present. Whatever he’d buried was surfacing now—not in words, but in the shake of his shoulders, the way he pressed a fist against his mouth like it might hold him together.

More flashes: a rainy afternoon, the two of them dancing in a kitchen. Her socks slipping on the floor. Him catching her mid-spin. The sound of their laughter layering like music.

I watched the monitor carefully. These weren’t standard grief hallucinations. They carried emotional weight and consistent physical cues. Eye color. Movement style. Even tone pitch remained stable across scenes.

Jonah’s breathing hitched, and tears slipped from beneath his closed eyelids. “I remember her. I know her. I didn’t imagine this.”

I wanted to offer comfort, but my throat closed up. Because I saw it too. I saw her. The girl. And my gut twisted because the shape of her face, the arc of her brow—it was too familiar.

One thread rippled violently. A fragment not yet fully formed pushed its way through the stream.

The memory darkened.

A crash. A scream. Jonah yelling. Running toward a shifting image of Lina lying motionless, her bracelet clutched tightly in one hand.

The bracelet.

I stepped forward instinctively. On the monitor, I could see it—white and teal beads, the same ones I’d worn as a child, the same ones buried in my keepsake box.

Jonah convulsed slightly as the sync stuttered.

“End sequence,” I commanded, fingers flying across the panel. The temperature inside the sync pod had spiked.

The machine groaned as it powered down, its cooling system whining. Jonah blinked furiously, wiping his face. “Why did you stop?”

“There was a destabilization,” I said, trying to keep my voice calm. “Memory fusion can create emotional feedback loops. We need to stabilize before attempting another session.”

He sat upright, gripping the chair’s arms. “She was there. I saw her again. And that bracelet. That was real.”

I nodded slowly, avoiding his eyes. “Yes. I saw it too.”

“Please,” he said, voice breaking. “We have to do one more. Go deeper. Pull more threads.”

I took a breath and stepped back. “Not today. I need time to recalibrate the system. And to think.”

“To think?”

“I’m starting to believe you, Jonah. But if we go in too fast, we risk corrupting the threads beyond recovery. We need to be careful.”

He stared at me like I was slipping away. “You don’t understand. Every minute I’m not in that chair, she’s further from me. Like she’s dissolving.”

My voice was barely a whisper. “She’s not gone.”

Jonah slumped forward, burying his face in his hands. I watched him for a moment longer than I meant to. His shoulders trembled with a grief that didn’t feel performative—it felt cellular, like something was unraveling from deep within.

Watching that unraveling did something to me. It cracked open the uneasy stillness I’d built around my own memory, my own childhood. My fingers hovered above the control panel, but my thoughts drifted backward—to dreams I couldn’t explain, to lullabies I swore I never learned, to a child’s laugh that sometimes echoed in my head late at night when I was alone.

I didn’t know Lina, not really. But the look in Jonah’s eyes made me wonder if a part of me had once known something… or someone… very much like her.

I powered down the last terminal, my hands lingering on the interface longer than necessary. The image of the bracelet and the child's eyes—so hauntingly familiar—wouldn’t leave my mind. My instinct said to report this, to tag it under anomalous data and let the Ministry protocols dictate the rest. But another part of me, quieter and older, whispered to keep it close.

I thought of the dreams, the lost time, the strange sense that something had always been missing. Naming the file wasn't just administrative—it was an admission. An acknowledgment that what I saw wasn’t just Jonah’s fragment. It belonged to me too, somehow. Lina. The name felt fragile and powerful at once, like saying it might summon something back. and placed the scan data into an encrypted drive. My fingers hesitated over the save label.

I didn’t write Jonah’s name. I didn’t write mine.

I labeled it simply: Lina.

As I walked out of the chamber, the overhead lights danced—not from power loss, but from resonance distortion. The kind that only happens when something deep, buried, and true is trying to surface.

Outside, the rain fell.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 – Static Zones
chapters.content:
Chapter 5 – Static Zones

I ducked beneath the magline archway just as static bit at the back of my tongue. The zone was deeper than I remembered. Past the city’s official grid, beneath a stack of decommissioned signal towers and an old magline station, the temperature dropped noticeably—cool, damp air brushing my skin like breath from an open crypt. The scent of rust and scorched circuitry clung thick in the air, mingling with the ozone tang of old static charges.

Dust tickled the back of my throat, and each footstep echoed faintly, absorbed by the matte walls padded in aged insulation. A low-frequency hum vibrated through the floor, a subterranean pulse that seemed to sync with my heart. I moved through the shadowy corridor, fingers trailing along the coarse wall, until the surface pulsed with pale green light—an artificial iris scanning my outline before the panel slid open.

Sami’s workshop was chaos incarnate—tangles of neural coils snaking across the floor, cracked data visors blinking erratically, and half-melted consoles emitting the acrid scent of old solder and ozone. The air buzzed with energy, like a hive perpetually on the verge of ignition. Surfaces were greasy to the touch, marked by smudged prints and scattered microtools. Code fragments blinked across half-working display screens in forgotten loops, shifting with corrupted lines of memory architecture.

As I stepped further in, I brushed past a bundle of hanging wires that swayed like seaweed, one brushing my cheek with a mild static shock. I ducked under a tilted drone arm bolted to the ceiling, its lens still glowing faintly, before reaching the center of the chaos. There sat a battered leather chair, its surface cracked and shiny with age, surrounded by projection nodes and a holographic canopy overhead, shimmering like slow lightning. Sami—part tech, part myth—was buried in code, her silver braid tied back with a soldering wire.

“Didn’t think I’d see you down here again,” she said without turning. “Last time nearly got me flagged. The Ministry swept my node bank for weeks. Thought you were done diving past surface layers.” “Last time you swore off deep registry dives.”

I stepped closer, placing the encrypted drive on her cluttered table. My hand hovered for a moment before letting go—an unconscious pause, the weight of what I was asking hitting harder than I’d expected. Part of me hesitated. Sami wasn’t just a fixer; she was my last unburned bridge to a world I wasn’t sure I still trusted. The last time I’d dragged her into Ministry shadows, she'd barely dodged a full neural audit.

I remembered the look in her eyes—calculated fear masked with sarcasm—and the way she’d said, "One day, your ghosts are going to cost us both." But this wasn’t just about ghosts anymore. It felt closer. More real.

“I need a silent audit. No Ministry channels. No traceable logs.” Sami finally looked at me. “Who pissed in your neural pool?”

“It’s not for me.” She raised a brow, then slid the drive into an analog port.

“What’s the  case?”

“Jonah Vale. Registry claims he has no family. No relational links. But he brought me a memory—one I shouldn’t have seen. It syncs with a child named Lina.”

Sami frowned, fingers flying across a holographic keypad. “Cross-referencing tags. Running delta-layer trace. This’ll take a sec.”

The room hummed with overlapping frequencies. I walked slowly, studying the walls plastered with old memory maps—some drawn by hand, others printed in fragmented layers like topography built from pain. I stopped at a crinkled photo tacked above a dusty panel—two boys, one blurred, the other smiling into a void.

Are those yours?” I asked.

Sami didn’t look up. “Everyone’s got ghosts. I keep mine close. Reminds me not to play god.”

Sami’s console pinged. “Found something,” she muttered. “Multiple overlapping hashes in his registry history. That’s not supposed to happen—not naturally.”

I stepped beside her. “What does it mean?”

“Someone’s rewritten his relational assignment blocks. Sloppy work too. Looks like an overwrite without proper emotional dissociation. He’s still linking—cortically and chemically—to the idea of a daughter.”

”Even without a record of her?” I asked.

Sami didn’t answer right away. I was already scrolling through the diagnostic sublayers, trying to trace the overwritten fragments.

My fingers stilled when a blinking signature popped up in the embedded metadata: ADDINGTON CASE: LOOP/NEURAL FAILURE (CLASSIFIED).

“What the hell...” I tapped it, pulling up the redacted header. “Sami, do you know this case?”

She leaned in and her expression tightened. “You pulled that from a Class 6? Damn. That file’s a graveyard.”

“So it’s real?” “Barely. Addington Loop’s one of those buried disasters. Officially, they called it a corrupted trauma loop—girl kept replaying the same memory sequence. Wouldn’t let  go. The techs tried to sever it, scrub the neural anchor, even install surrogate overlays. Nothing worked.”

I skimmed what little was left in the file. Most of it was redacted or garbled. A few surviving lines lingered: She’s still in there. Every time it resets, she remembers more. Loop unresolved.

“They said she broke four resonance techs,” Sami muttered. “One guy started dreaming about staircases for weeks. They wiped him before he could publish.”

I stared at the file. “She wasn’t malfunctioning. She was resisting.”

Sami looked at me sideways. “That’s one way to see it.”

A knot had formed in my chest, low and insistent. “And Jonah’s still linking emotionally... even without data.”

“Which means the Ministry didn’t just wipe him. They missed something.” She tapped the console. “Or someone didn’t want the wipe to hold.”

A shiver ran through me—tightness coiled just beneath my ribs, like a string being pulled taut. My hands tensed at my sides, and for the briefest moment, I heard a child’s laugh echo across memory, distant and half-forgotten. I swallowed hard, unsure if the sound was real or just the cruel trick of suggestion, but either way, it left me rattled.

“His cortex shows active bonding loops—especially in the deep limbic zone. That doesn’t happen unless the memory was reinforced over time.”

“Could someone have implanted Lina… for protective reasons?”

Sami leaned back, expression thoughtful. “Possible. Sometimes, when grief gets too destabilizing, the Ministry authorizes surrogate structures—false children, altered losses, manufactured closure.”

I swallowed. “So Lina might’ve never existed… but his pain is real.”

“Pain always is.” The console pinged again, flashing a red triangle. Sami frowned. “Here’s the kicker. There’s a tag embedded in his memory chain. It’s Ministry-coded… and time stamped six years ago.”

“But his files say his memory wipes are four years old.”

“Exactly. Someone’s hiding an earlier wipe.”

I felt like the floor shifted beneath me. A silent quake. Sami watched me. “You need to let this go. If you dig into relational reassignments, you’ll trigger flags. Audits. Worse.”

“I can’t. I saw the child. I saw her bracelet. And I’ve been dreaming about her since before Jonah walked in.”

Sami’s voice dropped. “You think this girl might be yours?”

“I don’t know,” I  whispered. “But if she is… someone didn’t just erase her from Jonah. They erased her from me too.”

The silence between us stretched. I sat on the edge of the console table, head in my hands. A quiet tension filled the room—the kind that buzzes louder than static. Sami moved to a back shelf, retrieved a battered journal, and tossed it to me. “Here. Use it. Analog’s safer. Start tracking what you’re seeing, what you’re dreaming. Names, symbols, anything weird.”

I caught the journal and thumbed through the pages—mostly blank except for a faded doodle on the inside cover: a child’s face, half-finished. The lines were jagged, drawn in a shaky hand, as if the artist had stopped midway or been interrupted. I ran my fingers lightly over the sketch, feeling the subtle grooves where pen had pressed into paper.

The paper was soft with age, edges curled and brittle. It smelled faintly of old ink and something harder to place—like dust and time baked into every fiber. I couldn’t stop staring at the single, unfinished eye. I imagined the rest of the face—how it might've looked, how it might still exist in a place I couldn’t reach. The silence around me deepened as something long-buried stirred behind my ribs.

Finally, Sami disconnected the drive. “I didn’t see this. You didn’t come here.”

I slipped the drive back into my coat. As I turned to go, a subtle movement caught my eye— a diagnostic panel on the far wall stuttered with static, its lights pulsing irregularly. For a moment, I thought I heard a faint, high-pitched whine—like an old comm channel trying to tune itself. I paused, head tilting toward the sound, but it vanished as quickly as it came.

Then she called out. “Lira?” I paused. “You ever wonder why we call them ‘false memories’ just because we can’t prove them?”

I didn’t answer. But I carried the question with me all the way back through the dark.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 – The Missing Girl
chapters.content:
Chapter 6 – The Missing Girl

I stood in the dark corner of my workspace, fingers flicking through layers of code on my personal terminal, eyes scanning for anomalies. The hum of the ventilation system blended with the low, steady thrum of the streetlights outside.

I wasn’t looking for Jonah this time. I was hunting a ghost—one I wasn’t even sure existed. I started with the Ministry’s public-facing memory archives, just to establish a baseline. But within minutes, I’d slipped into the backdoor channels I hadn’t touched in years. My fingers moved faster as I ran a scan for orphaned memory files—archived fragments assigned to minors with no attached guardianship.

The data dragged, slow and redacted, like it didn’t want to be found. A sluggish progress bar inched across the screen, and I tapped the desk with nervous fingers. That familiar smell of warm circuitry and brittle laminate insulation hung in the air, tugging old memories of sleepless Academy nights to the surface. Then everything stopped.

One line froze the interface—and my breath with it. LK-7. A sealed profile, flagged dormant. “Codename?” I muttered, voice thinner than I meant it to be. My fingers flew over the keys, triggering the metadata pull. LK-7. Level 6 clearance. Dormant for over a decade. No name, no guardian links, no medical overlay. Just a single chilling remark in the notes: “Containment advised until behavioral reconstruction is stabilized.”

The screen’s glow shifted as I leaned in closer. My own reflection blinked back from the dark glass—wide-eyed, mouth slightly open. It wasn’t just the clearance that rattled me. Something in that code rang like an echo, buried deep beneath all the wiped memories. And then it clicked. The file’s creation date. The exact same twelve-month gap in my personal records. The year my dreams turned to static. The year my school files picked up again without explanation. I tried to open the file. Static erupted across the screen, followed by a shrieking Ministry denial alert that pierced through the quiet.

I flinched as the interface lit up in a cascade of furious red. Tamper locks, biometric firewalls, time-keyed seals—layer after layer of digital barbed wire. The whole system convulsed, monitor pulsing like a seizure. My hands flew across the keys, rerouting my IP through a dead archive node. A dangerous trick—but the only one I had left.

When the system finally calmed, I sat back in my chair, chest heaving. My hands were trembling. That file hadn’t just been hidden. It had been buried. Quarantined. And someone wanted it to stay that way. Jonah’s words from the mosaic session came back to me: “The park… she liked the swings. There was a red kite. And a bench with initials.” I hadn’t thought much of it at the time. But now, it hit like a dropped memory fragment snapping into place.

I pulled up his last recorded session. The image of the carousel. The red kite. The initials carved into the bench. Not just a memory—a clue. Windmere Green. I typed it into my terminal, and something shifted. A phantom tug at the  back of my skull. The rush of air over a swing. The sharp scent of sun-warmed plastic. A child’s laughter—my laughter?—flickered at the edge of consciousness.

Windmere Green had once been a public sensory park. Seven years ago, it was quietly listed as decommissioned government property. No current zoning. No photo archives. But the map footprint still existed. I memorized it, a chill running beneath my skin like pages flipping too fast in my mind. That name… it didn’t feel like Jonah’s memory anymore. It felt like mine.

I debated bringing a drone but decided against it. If there were sensors, I wanted them to catch me, not a signal I couldn’t control.

I grabbed my coat, slipped a neural recorder disk into my pocket, and headed out into the night. By sundown, I stood at the edge of the old park. The fence was tangled in ivy, the chain links rusted to dust. My boots crunched over gravel and forgotten debris—bottle caps, beads, a broken toy soldier. The air smelled like mildew, rust, and something stranger. Like the ghost of a storm that never left. I found a weak spot in the barrier and ducked through.

The vines brushed cold against my neck. Moonlight cut through the trees in fragments, just enough to make out the skeletal remains of old play structures. A moss-covered slide. A jungle gym swallowed in bramble. The swings creaked in the wind, slow and mournful. Each breath I took tasted like dust and rain and memories I couldn’t quite name.

The carousel loomed ahead, its faded panels bowed like a crown too tired to stand. I stepped closer, and my chest tightened with something I couldn’t explain. A flash of metal caught my eye—a half-buried plate near a warped bench. I scanned for tripwires, motion triggers, then dropped to my knees, fingers reaching out on instinct. I didn’t even need to read the initials. I already knew. They were mine. Not just familiar—mine.

The version of me someone buried, erased, rewritten. It wasn’t a gravestone. Not really. But it felt like one. A marker for someone who used to exist. Someone I used to be. I couldn’t breathe. My hand hovered above the plaque, chest aching. Grief and awe tangled together, as if my body didn’t know which to feel first. My knees hit the soil, mud seeping through the fabric, grounding me in the moment.

This was real. I ran my fingers over the stone. It pulsed faintly with warmth beneath the dew, like it remembered, too. Bits of chipped blue paint clung to the edges. A faint impression beside it hinted something else had once rested there—maybe a keepsake, now long gone.

“Who were you to me?” I whispered.

The wind stirred, rustling the branches above like voices I couldn’t quite hear. I closed my eyes and listened. Not just to the silence—but to everything inside it. I didn’t feel alone in the park.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 – The Bracelet
chapters.content:
Chapter 7 – The Bracelet

Jonah was already waiting when I stepped into the clinic’s staff corridor, shoulders hunched like he was trying to fold himself into himself.

The overhead fluorescents buzzed faintly, one flickering in a tired, irregular rhythm. The air smelled like antiseptic and warm plastic. Somewhere down the hall, I caught the hiss of a sanitizing mist cycle starting up. The place felt too sterile, too clean—and Jonah looked like he carried something unclean into this vacuum-sealed world.

He held something in his hand—a small cloth pouch, frayed around the edges.

“I found it,” he said, skipping any kind of hello. His voice was low, rough. “It was in my old storage box. I’ve had it for years. Thought it was junk.”

I arched a brow. “So… you brought me a mystery trinket?” He opened the pouch carefully, like it might break. Inside was a child’s bracelet—just simple beads strung on worn cord. Pale blue. Soft white. A single pink heart carved from stone at the center.

The second I saw it, something inside me snapped open. A trapdoor memory. My lungs stalled—not from fear, but from a recognition so deep it bypassed logic altogether. “I’ve seen this,” I whispered.

“In the mosaic?” Jonah asked. “No,” I said, voice barely audible.

In my dreams.”

He nodded, slowly. “It was in a box of old stuff. I kept it in a storage unit my grandmother left behind—under some books, next to a cracked photo frame. I almost threw it out. I don’t even remember packing it.”

A memory surged forward before I could brace myself—small hands twisting the bracelet around a tiny wrist, the weight of goodbye, a voice cracking through tears. I blinked hard, trying to hold onto the image. Then I turned without another word and left the corridor.

When I got home, I tore through the bottom drawer of my memory box. My hands were shaking. The drawer was stuffed full of flattened neural tapes, warped report printouts, and old stim packets. I paused for a second when my fingers brushed over a keychain from school orientation and a faded name badge from my junior echoist internship.

For just a heartbeat, I was pulled back—into another version of myself I barely remembered. Then I saw it. Another bracelet. Identical. Same blue and white beads. Same heart-shaped charm. I stared at both bracelets for a long time, heart pounding unevenly in my chest.

The room around me faded to the edges, like I was standing at the rim of something too wide, too deep, to see all at once. The hum of the heating system buzzed in my ears—suddenly too loud, too close. I lifted the bracelet gently, rolling it between my fingers. The beads were smooth, worn. The pink heart chipped along one side. I brought it to my nose—it smelled faintly of dust and lavender. A scent I hadn’t realized I missed until that moment.

My vision blurred. I pictured sliding the bracelet onto a child’s wrist—my wrist? Lina’s? The phantom pressure of a small hand in mine lingered with haunting familiarity. When I closed my eyes, something else came. A scene. A farewell.

A child’s voice: “You won’t remember me, but I’ll remember you.”

A little girl with wide eyes and tangled hair, clutching the bracelet like it was everything she had left. A door closing. The taste of fear in my throat. A woman’s voice calling out, choked and distant.

And then Jonah’s voice again—echoing this time, clearer: “You won’t remember me…” I gasped and opened my eyes, throat tight with a sharp, aching twist of panic. What was happening to me? I stumbled into the bathroom and grabbed the sink. My reflection in the mirror looked wrong—eyes rimmed with confusion, skin pale and clammy.

I gripped the porcelain, counted my breathing in fours like I’d been trained to do after high-level scans. In. Hold. Out. Hold. My mind reeled. Were these memories actually mine? Or fragments bleeding in from Jonah’s grief? I thought about calling him. But what would I even say? That I was unraveling?  That something broken in him mirrored something broken in me?

Part of me wanted to shove it all back in the drawer, forget it ever happened. But something louder inside whispered: You already know. I slid to the floor. Both bracelets lay in my lap.

The edge of the sink was still warm where my hands had been. The tile beneath me felt cold and grounding. I rocked gently, the motion instinctive, as if my body needed to move to keep from fracturing. I reached for my journal. Flipped past clinical notes and archived session logs until I found a blank page. And on it, I wrote one word: Lina. I circled it. Stared at it. Underlined it twice.

A name. A ghost. A thread leading me back to something I hadn’t known I’d lost. Then I wrote: Where did you go? I scratched it out. Where did I go? I stood and crossed to my terminal.

Fingers trembling, I opened a new session file. Subject: Lina – Mosaic Sequence (Unscheduled) I hovered before submitting. Outside the window, something shifted—a bird maybe, or just the curtain catching a draft. But my skin prickled with unease. I typed one more line into the notes: Heart charm chipped—matches Jonah’s. Then, finally: If this is a dream, I don’t want to wake up .

I hit submit. I would find the truth. Or I’d break trying.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 – Rhea
chapters.content:
Chapter 8 – Rhea

The back entrance to the Memory Bazaar wasn’t marked, but I knew the pattern—two knocks, a pause, then a long press of my palm against the faded sensor. The alley reeked of old neural gel and sunbaked trash, but beyond the rusted door waited a world that pulsed with unauthorized memory work.  Inside, dim blue lighting twisted across the stained walls, casting warped shadows. Cables dangled from exposed ceiling vents like vines in some post-tech jungle. The floor buzzed beneath my boots—a subtle vibration, almost like the place had a heartbeat of its own.

I moved carefully, matching my steps to the rhythm of the flickering lights. Just past the threshold, the door sealed behind me with a hydraulic hiss. The air hit my tongue with the metallic taste of ionized dust and scorched silicon, laced with something sweet and rotten—fermented neural fluid, maybe. Every sound here was soft and sharp at the same time: whispered trades, the clink of memory shards, and low loops of fragmented code bleeding through open channels.

Rhea’s lab was in the far back, past whispering traders hawking illegal upgrades and hinting at "cleaned" identities. I slipped through a curtain fashioned from discarded neural shrouds and stepped inside. Rhea was hunched over a hologrid table, deep in her work. A projection of fractured memories hovered in the air—bits of laughter, blurred birthdays, half-formed faces blinking in and out like signal ghosts.

She didn’t look up. “I told you last time,” she said, fingers moving with practiced precision across the grid. “I don’t work with echoists.”

“I’m not here in that capacity,” I said. “This is personal.”

That got her attention. She straightened slowly, the streak of white in her dark hair catching the projection light. Her eyes were ringed with the kind of exhaustion you only get from diving too deep, too often, into things no one’s meant to see.

“Personal memory tampering?” she asked. “That’s even worse.”

I stepped closer and slid a scan capsule across the table. The projection flickered, then stabilized—there she was. A little girl with wide eyes, clutching a bracelet. My bracelet.

Rhea’s whole body shifted. She stopped what she was doing and leaned in, narrowing her eyes. “I’ve seen her,” she said softly. She rotated the image slowly. “Not in your file. This came from a client last year. Same face, different memory. The girl was crying on a bench. It was raining. She had no name. No origin tag.”

My breath caught. “You’re sure?”

“I pulled the scan and archived it,” Rhea replied, already digging through a cluttered drive case. “I was going to trace it, but the client vanished. Payment stopped. I figured the Ministry got to it."

She tapped a control. A second projection sprang to life. Blurry, but clear enough. Same girl. Same bracelet. Same expression that clawed at something just beneath my skin.

“This isn’t coincidence,” I said, barely above a whisper.

“No,” Rhea answered. “This is a reassign protocol. Rare. Dangerous. Someone was moved in the system—not just the memories, but identity itself.”

My stomach turned. “Can they do that?”

“They’re not supposed to,” she said. “But sometimes memory ghosts—those fragments you’ve been chasing—they show up when something goes wrong. You’ve been tugging on one.”

She stepped closer, her voice suddenly hard. “Listen to me, Lira. If you keep pulling this thread, it won’t just cost you your job. You’ll lose yourself.”

“I already have,” I told her. “I just didn’t know until now.”

We stood in silence, the image of the girl looping in slow, endless heartbreak. Eventually, Rhea turned away. “Take it,” she said. “But don’t come back.”

I took the scan. At the threshold, I paused. A nearby console sparked, then buzzed with a distorted voice loop: a child laughing—cut off abruptly. I spun, heart jumping into my throat. Nothing repeated. Just interference, I told myself. Just noise. I slipped back through the curtain.

The corridor’s shadows swallowed me. But as I stepped into the pulse-lit alley again, I clutched the scan tight to my chest. She wasn’t a phantom. She was real.  She was a thread. And I was going to follow her—no matter where it led.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 – The Memory Loop
chapters.content:
Chapter 9 – The Memory Loop

My fingers hovered above the console, the surface cool and humming faintly beneath my touch. That first session had rattled me more than I wanted to admit. It stirred fragments I couldn’t name and emotions I didn’t fully understand.

What if this went deeper? What if I wasn’t ready? A dozen questions tightened in my chest, but one surged above the rest: What if Jonah wasn’t the only one who had forgotten? I glanced at him—quiet, expectant, fragile in ways he didn’t show—and exhaled slowly.

“Okay,” I murmured to no one in particular. “Let’s see how deep this goes.”

The second mosaic session wasn’t like the first. From the moment the sync initialized, the emotional weight surged like a tidal current. I felt it before I even saw it—Jonah’s grief, raw and unfiltered, humming through the interface like static before a storm.

When the image of the girl started to form, her laughter wasn’t a gentle echo—it was a piercing cry that rang through my bones. Jonah’s breath hitched, and my fingers trembled at the console. This wasn’t just memory. It was mourning in motion.

As the sync deepened, the monitor pulsed red—not a warning, but a rare signal: shared resonance. A low-frequency hum filled the chamber, vibrating through my ribs like the breath of something ancient and alive. Threads of pale light spiraled down from the ceiling, pulsing in rhythm with my slowing heartbeat.

The air thickened, warm one moment, chilling the next, like memory itself was shifting the atmosphere. My vision shimmered—colors bent, sharp edges blurred—as my consciousness stretched outward, tethering to Jonah’s.

A soft click echoed behind my eyes, like a door unlocking. We weren’t just observing anymore. We were inside it. A shiver ran through me as our vitals aligned, our neural patterns overlapping. It wasn’t just observation. It was immersion. The world trembled and then reformed—a space we hadn’t entered alone, but both somehow recognized.

Lina turned her head and looked directly at us, her expression caught between recognition and confusion. My heart pounded. Jonah’s emotions threaded into mine—his love, his loss—and my confusion tangled with it like smoke.

The mosaic shifted again, textures warping like melting glass. Then, clarity. A dim room, enclosed and quiet, emerged. Dust hung motionless in a beam of light, and the scent of old paper, antiseptic, and something floral hit me like a forgotten scent I used to know.

Metal shelves lined the walls, stacked with neural drives. But it was the small cot in the corner that pulled my attention.

A whisper broke the silence—“Goodbye, Lina…”—soft, intimate, familiar. The voice echoed unnaturally, as though it bounced through every corridor in my mind. Jonah gasped beside me, breath ragged, his hand gripping the resonance table.

I turned. A tear rolled down his cheek. He stared at the room like it was a wound that never closed.

I froze, my body reacting before I understood. Something heavy settled behind my ribs. Not fear. Knowing. I’d just witnessed a memory he had never meant to share. In the corner, the girl sat cross-legged, humming softly. Then came a voice—not mine, not Jonah’s. Male. Familiar. It coiled around the room like smoke: “You won’t remember this. But I’ll remember you. Goodbye, little star.”

The lights dimmed. Lina didn’t cry. She just nodded once, like she’d already heard it before. And just like that, the ache of finality rooted in my chest like stone. Error alerts blinked across the interface. “Neural pattern misalignment,” one read. “Insufficient resonance stability.” The image stuttered. “The feed’s collapsing,” I muttered. “I need a real-time link to stabilize it.”

Jonah recoiled. “No. Not again.”

“Jonah, this mosaic is pulling something critical. If I don’t stabilize, we lose it.”

He shook his head. “It hurts. When you link that deep, I feel it all. The memory. The body. The fear. Her voice.”

I hesitated. “I can set it to passive. You won’t be fully in. Just... anchored.”

“You said that last time,” he whispered.

“I know,” I said gently. “But if we don’t do this, it ends here.”

He didn’t speak. Just nodded. I reached for the controls and synced our vitals. The scene  snapped back into focus.

Jonah stood in a sterile corridor, arms wrapped tightly around the girl—Lina. Her fingers clung to his collar, face buried in his neck. Across from him, a woman in a charcoal Ministry uniform waited, hands outstretched. Jonah whispered something into Lina’s ear, then, with shaking arms, passed her over.

Jonah’s breath hitched as the memory settled. He watched, frozen, as his past self-handed Lina to the woman. Lina clung to his shirt a beat too long. In the resonance loop, Jonah let out a sound—quiet, broken. His hands twitched. He wanted to reach through the memory, take her back. He gripped the chair, knuckles white. Regret poured across his face. “I didn’t want to,” he whispered. “I thought I’d get her back.”

Even as the memory dissolved, its weight settled into him like a stone .I felt it radiate from him. Grief. Not just remembered. Real. The moment fractured just as Lina looked back one final time.

Then something inside me broke. The image shimmered—a crumpled drawing taped to a wall. Crayon strokes. Stick figures. A crooked sun. And a name. Lina. The world narrowed. Sound faded. The letters weren’t just familiar. They were mine. The curve of the L. The jagged A. I’d written this. Or someone I used to be had. If I was Lina... who was Lira? My breath hitched.

The chamber pressed in. The past wasn’t something I reconstructed anymore. It was bleeding into me, rewriting me. I don’t remember drawing this, I thought. But my hands do. And suddenly, I wasn’t just remembering Jonah’s mosaic. I was living mine.

The chamber jolted. Lights flickered red and white. The hum rose into a screech. My console spat static. Heat warnings flared. Jonah’s restraints tightened.

“Abort sync!” I barked, hands flying over the controls.

Nothing. The images glitched, Lina’s face stuttering, disappearing. The temperature spiked. The scent of burnt wiring filled the air. I slammed the emergency switch. Everything stopped. The chamber groaned and went dark.

We gasped, like surfacing from deep water. Sweat dripped down my temple. Jonah’s shoulders shook. Our eyes met. No words. Just the raw, unmistakable fact: something had changed. Not in the mosaic. In us. The silence between us stretched, crackling with things we couldn’t say. I stood on unsteady legs and grabbed a half-crushed water bottle from the drawer. I handed it to him. Our fingers brushed. Neither of us acknowledged it. I didn’t ask if he was okay. He didn’t ask what I saw. The memory hovered between us like smoke.

“Whatever they took from us,” I whispered, “it’s still in there. Waiting to be remembered.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10 – Partition Drift
chapters.content:
Chapter 10 – Partition Drift

I couldn’t sleep—not with the fragments pulsing behind my eyes.

The memory loop had left something behind, a resonance I couldn’t shake. I sat curled on the floor of my tiny flat, the glow from my datapad casting shimmering light across the walls. I typed: Partition drift: theory or proven anomaly?

Dozens of scholarly articles populated the screen—most archived, redacted, or flagged with warning seals. The term referred to memory erosion after a forced wipe, when pieces of the past bled into present cognition like ink through a page.

I sifted through the literature. The deeper I dug, the more I found that matched Jonah’s case. Phantom recognition. Sensory imprints without context. Emotional residue that couldn’t be explained. Some cases included whispers heard in the dark, or smells that had no source but invoked deep longing or dread. I jotted frantic notes on a scratchpad beside me, sketching memory trails and resonance arcs.

Again and again, I circled one word: Lina. The name had begun to feel like a gravity well pulling me in. Eventually, I logged into an echoist relay network using a masked ID.

The forum was underground but active. I posted my questions carefully, omitting names. A few replies trickled in: one mentioned "emotional ghost loops," another referenced "unanchored protocols." No one used the name Lina. But then I got a private message: It’s not drift. It’s persistence.

My palms were sweating. I took a sip of synthetic mint tea and tapped my fingers against the glass rim, the click grounding me as anxiety crept in. The familiar hum of my apartment’s filtration system buzzed louder than usual—or maybe my nerves were amplifying everything. Just as I was preparing a follow-up, my comms console lit up.

Sami.

"Don’t talk. Just listen," Sami said, voice tight with urgency. "Your profile’s flagged. Noncompliance. I traced a Ministry ping—it’s trailing one of your files."

My breath caught. "Which one?"

"Doesn’t say. But it’s tied to off-protocol sync usage. You need to wipe your public terminal. Now."

"I can’t—Jonah’s scan—"

"Then move it. Off-grid. Use that old deck you keep behind the filtration panel."

I didn’t hesitate. I disconnected the neural bridge and ran to the wall. I pulled the panel free and revealed the dusty portable drive. My hands moved on instinct, slotting encrypted nodes, copying data, deleting traces. As the transfer bar crept forward, I caught my reflection in the black screen. My face looked thinner. Haunted. Not just tired—unraveling. Transfer in progress: 78%... 92%... Complete.

I hovered over the DELETE key. One tap, and all of it—Jonah’s fragments, Lina’s face, the mosaic—would vanish. Safer for him. Safer for me. But I didn’t move. Instead, I sealed the unit and slipped it into the lining of my field jacket. Moments later, my datapad buzzed.

1 New Message.

No sender. No return signal. Just five words: We remember you, Lina. I stared. My fingers trembled as I routed the signal through a localization trace. A ping bounced—off a ghost server, then another, before settling near the ruins of the Old Signal Tower.

I was out the door before my mind caught up. The city blurred past—concrete, static, sodium haze. My boots struck wet pavement as I ducked into the service corridors of the derelict sector.

The Signal Tower had long been gutted, stripped for parts, and buried in policy blackouts. But something buzzed behind the steel shell. A keypad blinked on as I approached. My presence activated it. I entered nothing. The door creaked open. A stairwell spiraled down into coded silence. The deeper I went, the colder it got and the older the walls became. Concrete pitted with rust and time. My breath frosted in the air. Machines stirred faintly as my steps echoed downward.

At the bottom, a single filament bulb lit a small room. Shelves lined the walls—reel tapes, analog drives, forgotten tech. The scent of ozone and dust settled around me. And someone was waiting. A figure stepped from the shadows, cloaked in neutral-gray. Their voice was soft but weighted: "You’ve come farther than most."

"Who are you?"

"We’re the ones who remember what the Ministry buries. And you, Echoist Kess," the figure tilted their head, "you’ve started to remember too."

I brushed cobwebs off an old console and asked, "You really work in here?"

The archive room was a forgotten pocket of time, carved beneath layers of city ruin and silence. Dust hung in suspended motes, dancing in the weak glow of a single overhead bulb. Rows of shelves groaned under the weight of aging paper files—some curled with moisture, others tagged with handwritten codes in fading ink. The air smelled of metal, mildew, and old circuitry, a scent like a locked drawer pried open after decades. Beneath my boots, the floor creaked with every cautious step, the boards warped and uneven.

Somewhere in the back, an analog server hummed with quiet insistence, like a machine still dreaming of purpose long after being forgotten. The contact—still nameless—lowered a rust-cracked file box onto the metal table between us. Their hood slipped slightly, revealing a pale cheek etched with faint neural scars—thin, silver filaments like faded circuitry running beneath the skin. Their voice had a clipped, melodic cadence, touched by an accent I couldn’t place—half-erased, like a borrowed memory. As they handled a nearby drive, their movements slowed, almost reverent, fingers brushing the case as though it contained a living thing.

"They took the children," they said, eyes never leaving the device. "Not to erase them, but to rewrite what couldn’t be endured."

"The Ministry didn’t just erase people," they said quietly. "They reassigned them."

I leaned in, watching as the lid creaked open. Inside were paper files, faded photo strips, hand-labeled drive chips.

"Back in the early cycles, they ran a pilot called Relational Reassignment Protocol. Children pulled from high-risk memory events—accidents, uprisings, illegal implants. Instead of letting the trauma play out, the Ministry severed the neural bonds, then rewired the emotional schema. Wiped them clean. Assigned them to new lives. New names. New families. And sometimes..." the contact slid a photo forward—blurry, but unmistakably a girl with dark eyes and a crooked smile, "the memories didn't stay gone."

I stared, my expression flat—but something inside cracked. I’d never seen that photo before, but my chest ached like it remembered. The contact continued, voice laced with something between pity and quiet fury.

“The theory was simple—trauma creates instability, so remove the root. Children of political prisoners, memory-burn victims, and classified test subjects were the primary targets. Once identified, their identities were scrubbed—birth records sealed, neural maps overwritten. Then they were inserted into pre-approved households as if they’d always belonged. Names changed. Birthdays reassigned. Even emotional memory templates were adjusted to mimic organic bonding.”

They paused, pulling out another file—a list of codenames beside cross-referenced civilian IDs. “It was called compassionate intervention. But what it really was?” The contact met my gaze. “Erasure by design.” The contact paused beside a battered crate of old registry logs, fingertips grazing the top. “There was a girl once—Anelise,” they said softly. “She’d been placed with a coastal family, new name, new life. But she kept drawing the same thing over and over: a burning stairwell, a mother calling her name from the smoke. The guardians thought it was imagination. Until the records surfaced—she’d survived a tower fire in the Western District. Her real mother had died trying to shield her.” Their voice dropped. “Some memories refuse to die quietly.”

I leaned in as the contact unfurled a yellowed datasheet, brittle at the corners. “Guardians were complicit—most unknowingly. After each reassignment, those involved were subject to enforced memory filtration. Not just the children—extended family, teachers, anyone who might question discrepancies. They were told it was for safety. That too much emotional residue risked destabilizing the child’s adjustment.” The contact tapped an old Ministry seal at the bottom of the page. “Some were willingly dosed. Others… were never given the choice. Forgetting wasn’t an accident. It was a mandate.”

My eyes drifted to the drive in the contact’s hand, but I didn’t reach for it. Instead, I focused on the analog terminal—dusty, half-functional, but still pulsing faintly with power. “Let me try,” I said, moving past the contact.

Before they could respond, I slid a cracked connector cable into place and pulled up the archival index. “Be careful,” the contact warned. “Some of these files are encrypted with legacy traps. Triggers meant to wipe or scramble under pressure.”

“I know,” I murmured. My voice was tight with urgency, with defiance. “But I need to see it myself.”

My fingers flew over the interface, bypassing obsolete firewalls and overlapping access codes. One folder refused to open—REASSIGN-LK-PROT47B. A red shield blinked beside the name. Unauthorized. Restricted. I hesitated for only a breath, then activated a system override. The console whined in protest. My heart pounded. The file trembled—then cracked open. Lines of green text flooded the screen—archives long thought lost or erased. My breath hitched as my eyes locked on the file labeled KESS, LINA – AGE 7.

My hands trembled as I reached for it, the edges of the folder rough against my fingertips. As I opened it, my vision swam—not from malfunction, but from the heat of unshed tears. A voice rang in my ears, faint and wavering, calling out “Lina, hurry!” My throat tightened as something long-buried clawed its way to the surface. I pressed a palm to my chest, trying to ground myself as the weight of it all settled in. Status: Reassigned. Guardian file: Jonah Vale.

The words seared  into my mind. It wasn’t just a theory anymore. It was me. A designation. A child reduced to a program line in a hidden ledger. I scrolled further. At first, the listing was clear: Guardian of Record – Jonah Vale. But then the text glitched—and the name blurred out, overwritten with Ministry jargon: REDACTED PER ORDER 47B.

I leaned in, watching as the system rewrote history in real time. A chill ran through me. This wasn’t deletion—it was deliberate erasure. Someone had tried to erase Jonah entirely from my file. The realization hit like a silent implosion. I stared at the screen, pulse thudding, as pieces of my identity aligned in ways they never had. I hadn’t been discarded—I’d been hidden. Protected.

The reassignment, the memory wipe, the falsified records—it wasn’t random. It kept me safe. And Jonah… he had known. He had helped. The weight of that knowledge twisted inside me—not just the loss of my past, but that someone had once cared enough to let me forget. My eyes lingered on the redacted line—Jonah’s name, barely visible  beneath the smear.

A tremor slid down my spine. Was it protection, or a violation? If someone erased my past to shield me, what did that say about who I was before? Did safety justify the loss of self? I pressed my palm against the cool edge of the drive, torn between gratitude and grief. Mercy or theft—it felt like both. The contact said little, but as I stared down at my own forgotten name, they rested a hand on my shoulder.

“We’re not just archives—we’re what remains,” they said.

The weight of it hit me—not just the data, the files, the fragments—but the people who carried them. Protected them. In that shared silence, I felt less alone. Not healed. Not whole. But connected. Anchored. I inhaled slowly, my fingers hovering over the interface. The data fragment labeled “LK-Reassign Partial” pulsed faintly, like a heartbeat under glass. I knew the risks—partition instability, emotional overload, system flags—but the pull was undeniable. If even a sliver of my original self remained buried in that file, I had to reclaim it.

I tapped the restoration protocol and whispered to the console, “No more forgetting.” The restore protocol blinked to life, code flooding the screen in bursts of green and gold. The lights in the room dimmed slightly, pulsing in sync with the system’s surge. Fragmented images stuttered across the display: a child’s silhouette spinning in sunlight, a hand reaching out, a drawing of a tree with two names in crayon. Audio crackled: static, then a whisper warped by time—“Li…na.”

My breath caught. The program pulsed one final time before stabilizing. The drive beneath my palm glowed faintly. What had been lost was no longer silent.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 – Fault Lines
chapters.content:
Chapter 11 – Fault Lines

I didn’t go straight home.

Instead, I walked. Past closed market stalls and rusting monorail lines. Past the blinking neon haze of static-scorched signs and shuttered terminals that hadn’t flickered to life in years. The whole city felt paper-thin—like if I pushed hard enough, it would tear and reveal the truth hiding underneath.

My legs carried me without direction, like they remembered something my mind hadn’t caught up to yet. I finally stopped at the shoreline, where wind lashed the rocks and seafoam churned against the pylons. The air smelled of brine and cold metal. I leaned against the weather-worn railing, the drive still in my jacket pocket, pressing against my chest like a second heartbeat.

The waves didn’t answer the questions circling in my mind. They just kept coming—relentless, like memory itself.

Jonah had known.

That was the part I couldn’t quiet. Not the Ministry’s cruelty. Not the program. But Jonah’s choice. To protect me. To erase me. What did that say about the life I’d lived before? That it had to be buried to keep me safe?

I wrapped my arms around myself and let the cold do what it could to numb me. It didn’t help. Some pain doesn’t freeze. It just waits.

Back at the flat, the air felt too still—like the room had been holding its breath in my absence. I powered up the old console hidden beneath the floorboards. The interface blinked awake slowly, as if reluctant to return to this world.

The restored fragment sat in the center of the screen. A tiny, pulsing icon. Waiting.

But I couldn’t open it again. Not yet. My fingers hovered over the command key, then dropped to my lap.

Instead, I opened a blank file.

I didn’t write like an echoist this time. I didn’t catalog. I confessed. To the screen. To myself. Fragments spilled out—partial dreams, old smells, broken imagery I couldn’t place but felt in my bones.

One stood out: a memory I hadn’t had until the file unlocked. A woman’s voice, muffled by smoke. “Lina, go!” A hand pushing me into light. The door slamming shut.

I wrote it down over and over, as if repetition could stitch the moment into permanence.

Later, I pinged Rhea through an encrypted relay node buried in an old academic server tree. I didn’t trust anything newer. The signal stuttered, caught, then connected.

Her face appeared on screen, grainy and sleep-creased. “Lira? What the hell time is it?”

“I found it,” I said.

That woke her up fast.

“Jonah’s file was real,” I continued. “I was reassigned. Protocol 47B. Lina Kess—age seven. Guardian: Jonah Vale. The system had redacted his name completely. Tried to wipe him from my record.”

She stared for a long moment, then whispered, “You always said something felt... off.”

“It wasn’t just instinct,” I replied. “It was memory. Residual. Partitioned.”

“Lira, are you okay?”

I hesitated. “I don’t know what that means anymore.”

Another pause. “What do you want to do?”

The question hovered in the air between us like a challenge.

I looked at the drive again. I thought about the contact in the archive, the old paper files, the names written in fading ink that someone had tried to erase.

“I want to find the others,” I said finally. “I want to wake them up.”

That night, I built a signal packet from scratch.

I didn’t use Ministry code. I didn’t even use my own ID. The message had to be clean. Undeniable. True.

I spliced the visual fragment from my own file—Lina’s name, the reassignment log, the redacted guardian line—and embedded it in a data shell. No commentary. Just the facts. A breadcrumb, for anyone who knew what to look for.

Then I encoded it with an old echoist tag: RELIC 7.

I routed it through the underground network—bounced across ghost relays, mirrored through dead net zones, and embedded in the metadata of a restored poetry manuscript. No one would find it unless they were already searching.

As the file uploaded, I whispered: “No more forgetting.”

The system logged it, timestamped it, and sent it into the dark.

When I shut everything down, the silence felt different. Not empty—pregnant. Charged. Like the moment before a system reboot.

I lay on the floor beside the console, watching the cracked ceiling above me.

Somewhere out there, someone might see that file and feel what I felt in the archive room. That flicker of impossible familiarity. That ache of almost-remembering.

And maybe they’d ask the same question I had.

Who was I before I was rewritten?

I pulled the drive close, curled my fingers around it, and closed my eyes.

Let them come for me now.

I’d remember my way through.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 – The Echoist’s File
chapters.content:
Chapter 12 – The Echoist’s File

I SAT CROSS-LEGGED on the floor, my portable console balanced across my knees. With the apartment lights dimmed and my comms link severed, I launched a ghost shell—an illegal patchwork of code stitched from old backdoor exploits and discarded Ministry protocols. My fingers flew across the screen, calling up encryption layers like stacked glass, each more fractured than the last.

Firewalls snarled to life, pulsing red across the interface as I wormed deeper into the system. A status bar froze at 97%, then blinked: Access Denied. My breath caught. I rerouted through a dead relay node, risking detection. For a heartbeat, nothing happened. Then—Access Granted.

A soft chime echoed as the file unfurled, and I exhaled shakily, slumping back as my heart pounded against my ribs like it was trying to escape. I sat alone beneath the hum of my portable rig, the terminal’s glow casting sharp lines across my face. My fingers flew over the interface, bypassing encryption layers that were never meant to be breached by those they were written about.

The file labeled KESS, L. – LEVEL 7 SEAL resisted my every override—until it didn’t. With a final keystroke, the lock crumbled. Dozens of entries spilled onto the screen: intake reports, psychological notes, memory sequence logs. A still image froze my breath—a scan of a younger me, eyes wide with something  between fear and wonder.

I’d become the echoist to study others’ pasts. I never imagined I’d be the most classified file of all. Among the unlocked records was a buried clip labeled simply: "Guardian Log 17B – J. Merren." I hesitated, then pressed

play. The screen flashed to life with static before settling on Jonah’s face—years younger, eyes hollowed with fatigue.

"If you’re watching this," he began, voice low, "then the seal was broken—and you’ve remembered too much." He looked away, then back. "They told me to forget you. Said it was for your safety. But I couldn’t. Not really." His voice cracked. "You were mine to protect, Lina. I tried. I’m  sorry."

"I didn’t want to," he whispered, the words unprompted. "I thought I’d get her back." His voice wavered, but he didn’t look away. "They said she wasn’t safe. That someone from her origin slate was flagged—parental dissident classification, subversive memory markers. They said if we kept her, she’d be a liability. That she'd either vanish… or I would."

He drew in a shaky breath. "They gave me a choice I was never meant to survive. Let them reassign her quietly, or keep her and watch her disappear without warning. I thought—if I followed the rules, at least she’d stay alive." In the final seconds of the confession video, Jonah’s voice grew softer, barely more than a whisper, as he pressed a trembling hand to his temple. "She’ll be safer if she forgets," he said, eyes glistening with unshed tears. "I’ll take the pain so she doesn’t have to."

The words struck like a blade—quiet, resolute, and full of love. I felt them settle in my chest, not just as a statement, but as a sacrifice. It wasn’t just a decision made by a guardian—it was a vow. One that had cost us both everything.

The screen wavered as the confession video began, casting a pale glow across my face in the darkened room. Static hissed faintly in the background, and the edges of the footage  wavered like an old memory trying to hold shape.

Jonah sat in a shadowed corner, the lighting dim and uneven—half his face illuminated, the other lost in gloom. A low hum buzzed beneath his voice, the sound of ancient hardware straining to play the file. The timestamp blinked in and out, corrupted. Every few seconds, the image glitched, lines rippling across his form as if even the data resisted remembering. Jonah’s face appeared gaunt on the screen, eyes rimmed with exhaustion and something heavier—regret, maybe, or quiet desperation. His usually composed demeanor had cracked; his shoulders slumped, and a deep line creased his brow.

When he spoke, his voice was low and uneven, like each word cost him something. There were pauses—too long to be accidental—where he seemed to debate continuing, mouth opening only to close again. At one point, he blinked rapidly, and for a moment, it looked like tears welled before he forced them back. This wasn’t the Jonah I knew—it was a man unraveling for the sake of someone else.

As the final frames of the video faded out, I sat motionless, the silence pressing in.

The weight of Jonah’s words coiled tightly around my chest. My memories hadn’t been stolen in some cold bureaucratic sweep—they had been surrendered. Offered up willingly, like a torch passed in the dark. Not ripped from my mind, but gently laid to rest so I might live without fear, without pain. That realization hit harder than any violation. Because it meant I had been loved deeply—enough for someone to let me go entirely.

The lights in my apartment were dim, the only illumination coming from the static-blue glow of the paused video screen. I sat curled on the floor, knees drawn to my chest, the surrounding silence broken only by the hitch of my breath. Tears fell freely now—hot, silent, relentless. They weren’t just for what I’d lost, but for what had been given up for me. For Jonah. For Lina.

The apartment felt like a museum of stillness. The overhead light buzzed faintly, casting dull shadows over stacks of untouched memory tapes and tea gone cold beside me. A forgotten photo strip curled at the edge of the desk—three blurred smiles, one unmistakably mine, though I couldn’t place the day.
